Physical investigation of [[Outer space|outer space]] by uncrewed robotic probes and by human spaceflight. Astronomy predates recorded history, but large, efficient rockets of the mid-20th century made direct exploration possible. Stated rationales include scientific research, national prestige, uniting countries, ensuring humanity's long-term survival, and military and strategic advantage.

The first recorded telescopic astronomy was by [[Galileo Galilei]] in 1609; the Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, set a later milestone. The early era was driven by the [[Space Race]] between the Soviet Union and the United States. The Soviet Union launched [[Sputnik 1]], the first human-made object to orbit Earth, on October 4, 1957, and achieved many early firsts: the first living being in orbit in 1957, the first human spaceflight (by [[Yuri Gagarin]] aboard Vostok 1) in 1961, the first spacewalk (by Alexei Leonov) on March 18, 1965, the first soft landing on another celestial body (Luna 9) on February 3, 1966, and the first space station, Salyut 1, in 1971. The United States achieved the first crewed Moon landing with [[Apollo 11]] on July 20, 1969; six crewed landings took place, the last in 1972.

In the 1970s, focus shifted from one-off flights to reusable hardware such as the Space Shuttle, and from competition to cooperation, the foremost example being the [[International Space Station]], built between 1998 and 2011. China, the European Union, Japan, and India advanced their programs in the 2000s, and private launch vehicles, capsules, and satellite manufacturing rose in the 2010s. Robotic probes such as the Voyagers have mapped the outer planets and entered interstellar space, in 2012 and 2018. In the 2020s, the two leading programs are Moon-focused: the U.S.-led Artemis program and the Chinese-led International Lunar Research Station, each with international partners.

Flight of objects, usually spacecraft, into or through [[Outer space|outer space]], with or without humans aboard. Most spaceflight is uncrewed, conducted with satellites in Earth orbit and with space probes beyond it, under telerobotic or autonomous control. Human programs include Soyuz, Shenzhou, the past Apollo Moon landings, and the Space Shuttle; current crewed flights go to the [[International Space Station]] and China's Tiangong station.

Spaceflight is achieved conventionally with multistage rockets. Once a spacecraft reaches sufficient speed it falls around Earth rather than back to the surface, which defines orbit. Debris from spent stages and failed spacecraft threatens working satellites, a cascade known as Kessler syndrome.

The first theoretical proposal of rocket space travel was published in 1861 by William Leitch. Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's 1903 work set out the rocket equation, still used by engineers. [[Robert H. Goddard]] published *A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes* in 1919 and launched the first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16, 1926. During World War II, Nazi Germany developed the [[V-2 rocket]], the first guided rocket, which became the first human-made object to reach space. Most of its team, including [[Wernher von Braun]], surrendered to the United States. Sergey Korolev's R-7 missile derivatives launched [[Sputnik 1]], the first artificial satellite, on October 4, 1957. [[Yuri Gagarin]] flew Vostok 1 in 1961. President John F. Kennedy pledged to reach the Moon, leading to the Gemini and Apollo programs and the crewed lunar landing of [[Apollo 11]] on July 20, 1969.

The Space Shuttle program operated from 1981 to 2011 and conducted 135 missions. Reusable rockets have since reshaped launch economics; SpaceX's Falcon 9 has achieved over 300 successful launches by 2025, and the company's Starship is aimed at goals such as Mars colonization.

Country in Southern and Western Europe with territories in North Africa (pop., 2026: 49.8 million). Spain covers 505,983 sq km, most of the [[Iberian Peninsula]], and includes the Canary Islands, the Balearic Islands, and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla. It borders France, Andorra, Portugal, and Morocco. The capital and largest city is [[Madrid]].

The peninsula was home to Iberians, Celts, and other peoples before Roman conquest created the province of Hispania. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the Visigoths established a kingdom centered on Toledo. In the early 8th century the Umayyad Caliphate conquered most of the peninsula, creating [[Al-Andalus]] centered on Córdoba. Northern Christian kingdoms launched the [[Reconquista]], which ended with the fall of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada. The 1479 dynastic union of the Crowns of Castile and Aragon under the Catholic Monarchs is often seen as the de facto unification of Spain as a nation state.

During the Age of Discovery Spain led the exploration and conquest of the New World and built the [[Spanish Empire]], ruled by the Habsburg and Bourbon dynasties. The 19th century brought the victorious Peninsular War (1808–1814) and the loss of most American colonies. Conflicts culminated in the [[Spanish Civil War]] (1936–1939) and the dictatorship of [[Francisco Franco]] (1939–1975). A constitution adopted in 1978 established parliamentary rule and regional autonomy, and Spain joined the [[European Union]] and NATO.

Spain is a secular parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, with King Felipe VI as head of state. It is a unitary state of 17 autonomous communities; regional tensions, particularly in Catalonia, remain a political issue. Spanish is the national official language. Spain has a developed, high-income economy, the fourth largest in the European Union.

Global colonial empire, 1492–1976, ruled by the Crown of Castile and later by unified Spain. With Portugal, it ushered in the European [[Age of Discovery]], and it was known as "the empire on which the sun never sets." At its greatest extent, in the late 1700s and early 1800s, it covered 13.7 million sq km.

The empire began with the 1492 arrival of [[Christopher Columbus]], sponsored by Isabella of Castile after the Catholic Monarchs completed the conquest of Granada. The [[Treaty of Tordesillas]] (1494) divided the world between Spain and Portugal, giving Spain the Western Hemisphere. Spain expanded across the Caribbean, half of South America, most of Central America, and much of North America. Hernán Cortés defeated the [[Aztec Empire]] in 1521, and [[Francisco Pizarro]] overthrew the Inca Empire in 1533. From 1580 to 1582 Spain conquered Portugal, creating the Iberian Union, which lasted until 1640.

Silver and gold from mines at Zacatecas, Guanajuato, and Potosí enriched the crown and financed wars and expansion. Colonial rule operated through viceroyalties and audiencias under the Laws of the Indies (1573); the New Laws of 1542 sought to curb abuses of the encomienda system. Historians differ on how much colonial revenue reached Spain: critics stress extraction, while others note large local spending on civil and military needs within the colonies.

Bourbon rule, from 1700, brought the Nueva Planta decrees and centralization. Tensions between peninsular Spaniards and Creoles, and [[Napoleon]]'s 1808 invasion of Spain, set off independence wars that, by the mid-1820s, cost Spain Mexico, Central America, and South America. After the [[Spanish–American War]], it lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and Guam by late 1898. The empire ended with Spain's withdrawal from Western Sahara in 1976.

[[Romance languages|Romance language]] of the Indo-European family, spoken natively mainly in the Americas and Spain. Also called Castilian (*castellano*), it evolved from the Vulgar Latin of the Iberian Peninsula and originated in the [[Kingdom of Castile]], in what is now north-central Spain. It is the world's second-most spoken native language after [[Mandarin Chinese]] and its most widely spoken Romance language. Estimates of native speakers range from 498 million to 519 million. It is an official language of 20 or more countries and one of the six official languages of the [[United Nations]]. [[Mexico]] has the most native speakers, about 130 million.

Spanish descends from Vulgar Latin, which reached the peninsula with the Romans during the Second Punic War, beginning in 210 BC. The first documents showing traces of Spanish date from the 9th century, and the first systematic written use took place in Toledo in the 13th century. About 75% of modern vocabulary is Latin in origin. It borrowed words from neighboring Romance languages, Andalusi [[Arabic]], and Basque. Spread through the Catholic Monarchs' unification and the [[Spanish Empire]] made it dominant across the Americas and into parts of Africa, Asia, and Oceania, though its global reach stems from colonization.

In Spain the language is called both *español* and *castellano*, the latter contrasting it with Galician, Basque, Catalan, and other languages of Spain. The 1978 Constitution uses *castellano* for the official language of the state. The Royal Spanish Academy, which has standardized the language since 1713, called it *castellano* from 1713 to 1923 and now prefers *español*, while regarding both terms as valid. According to the Academy, *español* derives from Occitan *espaignol*, from Vulgar Latin *hispaniolus* ("of Hispania"). Its literary tradition includes *Don Quixote* by [[Miguel de Cervantes]].

Basic unit of biological classification, a [[Taxonomic rank|taxonomic rank]], and a unit of [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]]. The best-known definition, the biological species concept, describes a species as the largest group of organisms whose appropriate sexes or mating types can produce fertile offspring, usually by sexual reproduction. Ernst Mayr formalized it in 1942, emphasizing reproductive isolation. Every species receives a two-part binomial name: the [[Genus|genus]] followed by the specific epithet, as in *Boa constrictor*. The most recent rigorous estimate of the number of eukaryote species is 8 to 8.7 million, of which about 14% had been described by 2011.

No definition is fully satisfactory. Species concepts also rest on karyotype, DNA sequence, morphology, behavior, or ecological niche; scholars have counted between about 24 and 26 distinct concepts. The morphological concept is useful for fossils but can mislead through convergent evolution. The phylogenetic concept defines species as the smallest monophyletic groups, and the ecological concept, proposed by Leigh Van Valen in 1976, views a species as a lineage adapted to a particular niche. Boundaries blur through [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] and ring species, and among asexual organisms each clonal lineage is potentially a microspecies. Viruses are treated as quasispecies. Despite this "species problem," the concept remains a useful tool for scientists and conservationists, and legal protections such as the Endangered Species Act depend on it.

From [[Aristotle]] until the 18th century, species and higher taxa were seen as fixed categories in a hierarchy, the great chain of being. In the 19th century biologists recognized that species evolve. [[Charles Darwin]]'s 1859 book *On the Origin of Species* explained how they arise by [[Natural selection|natural selection]], and 20th-century genetics and population ecology extended that understanding.

Use of the human voice as a medium for [[Language|language]]. Spoken language combines [[Vowel|vowel]] and [[Consonant|consonant]] sounds into units of meaning such as words. Speakers perform many intentional [[Speech act|speech acts]], including informing, declaring, asking, persuading, and directing, varying enunciation, intonation, loudness, and tempo to convey meaning. Speech also unintentionally reveals traits such as age, origin, and education. Some psychologists, such as [[Lev Vygotsky]], hold that silent inner speech helps organize cognition.

Normal speech is pulmonic: pressure from the lungs sets the glottis in the larynx vibrating, and the vocal tract and mouth shape the sound into vowels and consonants. Production is an unconscious, multistep process in which the speaker selects words from the lexicon, organizes them through syntax, retrieves their phonetic properties, and articulates them. Articulatory [[Phonetics|phonetics]] classifies sounds by place and manner of articulation. Speech errors are common, especially in children, and are used to build models of language production and acquisition. Children's over-regularizing of the English past tense ("singed" for "sang") suggests that regular forms are acquired first. Errors in [[Aphasia|aphasia]] have helped map components of speech onto the brain, including Broca's area and Wernicke's area.

Speech is studied by linguistics, cognitive science, communication studies, psychology, computer science, speech pathology, otolaryngology, and acoustics. It differs from written language in vocabulary, syntax, and phonetics, a situation called [[Diglossia|diglossia]].

The evolutionary origin of speech is debated. Although animals communicate by vocalization, and trained apes such as Washoe and Kanzi can use simple sign language, no animal's vocalizations are articulated phonemically and syntactically. No monkey or ape uses its tongue for sound production. The vocal tract does not fossilize, and indirect fossil evidence of changes to it has proved inconclusive.

Speed at which electromagnetic waves travel; in a vacuum, a universal physical constant denoted *c*, exactly 299,792,458 m/s. The value is exact because, by international agreement, the [[Metre|metre]] is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Before 1983 the metre was defined separately and the speed of light was measured experimentally.

All [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]], massless particles, and field perturbations such as [[Gravitational wave|gravitational waves]] travel at *c* in a vacuum, and the speed is the same for all observers regardless of the motion of the source. It is the upper limit for the speed of information, matter, or energy. Particles with mass can approach *c* but never reach it. Light travels more slowly in materials. The ratio of *c* to its speed in a medium is the [[Refractive index|refractive index]], about 1.5 for glass, so light in glass travels at roughly 200,000 km/s. Apparent faster-than-light recession of distant galaxies arises from the expansion of the universe, since only local velocity is uniquely defined.

Ole Rømer first showed that light is not instantaneous, by studying delays in the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io. In an 1865 paper [[James Clerk Maxwell]] proposed that light is an electromagnetic wave travelling at *c*. [[Albert Einstein]] postulated that *c* is constant in every inertial frame and independent of the source's motion; from this he derived [[Special relativity|special relativity]], in which *c* links space and time and appears in the [[Mass–energy equivalence|mass–energy equivalence]], E = mc². The origin of the symbol *c* is unclear; it may stand for "constant" or for the Latin *celeritas* ("swiftness").

Seed, fruit, root, bark, or other plant substance used primarily for flavoring or coloring food. Spices are distinguished from [[Herb|herbs]], the leaves, flowers, or stems of plants used for flavoring or garnish; both are seasonings. Spices are sometimes used in medicine, religious rituals, cosmetics, and perfume, and plant sweeteners such as sugar are not counted among them. A whole dried spice keeps longest, while a fresh spice such as ginger is usually more flavorful but costlier and shorter-lived. A 2019 review found that most claimed health benefits were not supported by clinical evidence, though it noted that polyphenols in spices may be beneficial. India contributes 75% of global spice production.

Defining spice is difficult. The *Oxford English Dictionary* places spices in the tropics, but caraway shows that they can come from temperate climates, and *The Oxford Companion to Food* notes that ambergris, of animal origin, is often called a spice.

Spices were used in small quantities, leaving few archaeological remains. A spice trade across the Indian subcontinent and the Middle East existed by 2000 BC, in [[Black pepper|black pepper]] and [[Cinnamon|cinnamon]]; [[Clove|cloves]] were used in Mesopotamia by 1700 BC. Discovery of the [[Monsoon|monsoon]] winds enabled sea trade to replace overland caravan routes. Spices appear in the Old Testament, and Pliny the Elder wrote about cloves. In medieval Europe they were among the most demanded and expensive goods, valued for balancing the "humors" under [[Humorism|humorism]] and for their association with "paradise." European demand helped drive exploration in the early modern period. [[Vasco da Gama]] reached India by sea in 1498, and European powers established outposts in spice-producing regions such as the [[Maluku Islands]].

Personal pursuit of meaning, purpose, and connection to a sacred or transcendent dimension of existence, a term whose sense has shifted over time. Traditionally it denoted a [[Religion|religious]] process of re-formation that "aims to recover the original shape of man," oriented toward "the image of God." According to Kees Waaijman, the model is the Torah in [[Judaism]], Christ in [[Christianity]], the Buddha in [[Buddhism]], and the Prophet Muhammad in [[Islam]].

The word derives from Latin *spiritus* ("breath," "soul," "courage"), which the Vulgate used to translate Greek *pneuma* and Hebrew *ruach*. Words translatable as "spirituality" appeared in the 5th century and entered common use late in the Middle Ages. In early Christianity it meant a life animated by the Holy Spirit. In the 11th century it came to denote the mental aspect of life against the material and sensual. In the 13th century it acquired social and psychological senses: the territory of the clergy as against secular authority, and the realm of the inner life. In the 17th and 18th centuries it was associated with [[Mysticism|mysticism]] and quietism and took on a negative meaning.

Modern notions developed through the 19th and 20th centuries, mixing Christian ideas with [[Western esotericism]] and elements of Asian, especially Indian, religions. Modern usage stresses subjective experience and the "deepest values and meanings by which people live," often apart from organized religion. It may involve belief in a supernatural realm, personal growth, religious experience, or a search for one's "inner dimension". No single definition is agreed on; scholarly surveys find a broad range of definitions with limited overlap. Studies link spirituality with health benefits, but critics note that these associations are correlational and rely on self-reported data.
